question_en: A large corporate issuer issued $50 million to the general public in a new bond offering two years ago. Using the same offering circular, the company just issued an additional $30 million in new bonds, most likely due to a:
explanation_en: Shelf registration A single, all-encompassing offering circular Can last for years, covering multiple new issues Securities can be issued with just a short document confirming details have not changed Allows issuer flexibility to quickly issue securities when conditions are favorable A shelf registration gives certain well-established issuers the ability to file a single, all-encompassing offering circular (ie, master prospectus) that allows securities to be issued quickly in the future when capital is needed or when market conditions are favorable. The term comes from the idea that the securities are "sitting on a shelf," just waiting to be sold. Shelf registrations can last for years, and all that is required for a new issuance is a short document confirming that no material changes have occurred that require additional disclosure. (Choice B) A private placement is not sold to the general public, and the investors would most likely require a new prospectus. (Choice C) A best effort offering is a type in which the broker sells securities only on a "best effort" basis. It is typically used only for high-risk securities, not those from well-known, seasoned issuers.

question_en: An analyst is classifying bonds within the global fixed income market. Which of the following is least likely a valid distinction for the analyst to use?
explanation_en: Fixed income securities can be classified in a number of different ways; the most common classifications are shown above. Bilateral and syndicated are types of loans, not types of bonds, made by banks to corporations and other entities. A bilateral loan is made from a single lender to a single borrower who needs funding. A syndicated loan is made by a syndicate (ie, a group of lenders who share the credit risk of the loan). Note that although a bond issuance may, in some cases, be purchased by a single institutional investor, this bond is not called "bilateral." (Choice B) Bonds may be classified by coupon type, so fixed versus floating is a valid distinction. The "rate" refers to the coupon rate paid by the issuer, so fixed-rate bonds maintain the same rate or coupon over time. Floating-rate bonds have a rate that varies based on a reference rate such as LIBOR. (Choice C) Bonds may be classified by issuer type, so corporate versus nonsovereign is a valid distinction. There are four broad bond sectors: financial institutions, nonfinancial corporates, governments, and households. Within the government sector, nonsovereign bonds are issued by authorities (eg, municipal governments) subordinate to national governments.

question_en: Typically, corporate bonds are most likely issued through a(n):
explanation_en: Corporate bonds are most often issued in an underwritten offering; this is also known as a firm commitment offering. In an underwritten offering, the underwriter (eg, investment bank) guides the issuer through the issuance process (eg, size, structure, pricing) by conveying investors' preferences. The underwriter then buys the entire issue to resell to investors, thus guaranteeing that the issuance is successful for the issuer but taking a financial risk if not all the bonds are sold. (Choice A) Auctions utilize a bidding process for price discovery and are more typical in the issuance of sovereign government debt. Sovereign bonds are well known to investors; combined with the standardized nature and regular issuance of these bonds, they enable the lowest cost issuance method, namely an auction. (Choice B) In a best effort offering, the investment bank is acting only as a broker and will sell the issue only on a "best efforts" basis for a commission. Best effort offerings are not as common and usually reserved for high-risk issues.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\7. Fixed Income\7.03 Fixed-Income Issuance and Trading - Answers.pdf
question_en: The secondary market for a particular bond is most likely deemed liquid if the bond can be sold quickly:
option_c: at close to fair market value.
explanation_en: Secondary bond market liquidity Not simply about how quickly a bond can be bought or sold The ability to buy and sell quickly at prices close to fair value The secondary bond market is dominated by institutional investors and central banks, with only limited retail participation. Securities are most often traded through a broker-dealer in over-the-counter (OTC) transactions. Outside of a handful of very liquid bonds (eg, sovereigns) that can be traded on an electronic order execution system (ie, "screen"), the liquidity of bonds is largely dependent on getting manual quotes from brokerage firms. Secondary bond market liquidity is determined by both how fast a bond can be bought or sold and how closely the price approximates fair value. For example, suppose an institutional investor is interested in selling a high-quality bond and, due to the decentralized nature of the OTC market, the investor requests bids (ie, price the buyer is willing to pay) from numerous brokerage firms (ie, manual quotes). Depending on the bond and market conditions, the price dispersion may be quite wide. In this case, suppose the best bid received is 2% below what the investor believes is a fair market price. This bond would not be considered liquid in the sense that even though the bond can be sold quickly, the price is too far below fair market value. (Choice A) Numerous bidders alone do not constitute a liquid market, particularly if the bids are materially below fair value. (Choice B) The market convention for settling most corporate bonds is trade date plus two or three days (eg, t + 3). Same-day settlement is often possible, but it frequently comes at a price further from fair market value, indicating a less liquid market.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\7. Fixed Income\7.03 Fixed-Income Issuance and Trading - Answers.pdf
question_en: Floating rate notes (FRNs) are most likely issued by banks to:
explanation_en: Floating rate notes (FRNs) are most often issued by banks to align balance sheet interest rate risk. FRNs are generally issued with short-term maturities and are frequently tied to the same reference rates as an institution's liabilities. By matching the interest rate risk of assets and liabilities, the bank diminishes earnings and net worth fluctuations, thus decreasing the probability of an adverse outcome on a financial institution's capital buffer. (Choice B) Banks and corporations issue FRNs for different purposes and needs. Corporate borrowers will issue FRNs as an alternative to bank lines of credit when financing is cheaper. Corporate issuers may also speculate on the direction of interest rates, issuing FRNs when they believe interest rates will fall. (Choice C) FRNs are most often issued with short maturities to align interest rate risk at banks. Long-term funding is largely secured through other means (eg, fixed rate debt, preferred stock).

question_en: A dealer places a noncompetitive bid in a single-price auction of government bonds for $1 million face value of bonds. Which of the following statements most accurately describes the amount of bonds the dealer will receive when the auction is concluded?
option_a: None, since the bid is noncompetitive
option_b: $1 million face value of bonds at the issuer-accepted yield
option_c: $1 million face value of bonds at the yield that the dealer bid
explanation_en: Governments often issue bonds through an auction. Bidders submit bids that specify the lowest yield that they will accept for a specified amount in bonds. For instance, a dealer may bid a yield of 3% for $10 million face value of two-year bonds. Bids are ranked from lowest to highest in terms of yield, but the yield accepted by the issuer is usually some type of average from the bids submitted. A single-price auction means that all winning bidders pay the same price for the bonds (ie, they receive the same yield). Bids can be submitted on a competitive or a noncompetitive basis. Competitive bidders may not receive bonds if their bids are higher than the lowest accepted yield. (Choice A) A noncompetitive bid means that the bidder simply wants bonds, regardless of price. Noncompetitive bidders agree to take bonds at the issuer-accepted yield, so they always receive bonds from the issue. (Choice C) A single-price auction means that all winners receive bonds at the same price, regardless of the price that they submitted. In a multi- price auction, winning bidders receive bonds at the yield that they bid, so winners pay different prices.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\7. Fixed Income\7.03 Fixed-Income Issuance and Trading - Answers.pdf
question_en: With respect to the supply of fixed-rate and floating-rate debt, which of the following statements is most accurate?
option_a: Consumer banks prefer to make fixed-rate loans.
option_b: Consumer finance companies prefer to issue floating-rate debt.
option_c: Corporate borrowers expecting higher rates prefer to issue floating-rate bonds.
explanation_en: The supply of fixed-rate and floating-rate debt results from lenders attempting to match the type of interest rate they receive from assets to the type of interest rate they pay for liabilities. In general, institutions seek to match fixed to fixed and floating to floating since doing so mitigates interest rate risk. Consumer finance companies extend short-term loans, so the interest earned on their loan assets may vary greatly over time. Therefore, these companies prefer to issue floating-rate debt to finance their own operations. (Choice A) Consumer banks are funded by accepting checking (ie, demand), savings, and money market deposits from customers and by selling certificates of deposit. These short-term sources are liabilities for the bank, and their rates change frequently. To match their interest patterns, banks prefer to make floating-rate loans. (Choice C) Corporations expecting lower interest rates prefer to issue floating-rate bonds so their future financing costs will be lower.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\7. Fixed Income\7.03 Fixed-Income Issuance and Trading - Answers.pdf
question_en: A bond that trades in the secondary market is most likely transacted:
explanation_en: While some government and very active corporate bonds do trade on an exchange (Choice B), the great majority of bonds are bought and sold in the over-the-counter (OTC) markets. An exchange is a central location where all orders are processed, whereas the OTC markets have no specific location: buyers and sellers are connected by various trading platforms that form a communications network. (Choice A) Auctions are primarily used with new-issue sovereign government bonds.

question_en: A Japanese corporation makes a public offering of EUR-denominated bonds in the French domestic bond market. From a French investor's perspective, these securities are most likely considered:
explanation_en: Geographic classification of bonds Domestic bonds Foreign bonds Eurobonds Issuer Same as country Different from country of issuance domicile of issuance Currency Domestic (local) currency Foreign currency Jurisdiction Domestic legal, regulatory, and tax rules Numerous exemptions Foreign bonds are debt securities issued in the domestic market by foreign-domiciled issuers. The securities are denominated in the local currency and are subject to local laws, regulations, and taxes. Foreign issuers issue such securities to reduce currency risk for earnings of domestic subsidiaries and/or to gain access to capital at attractive interest rates. In this scenario, the debt of the Japanese corporation issued in France and denominated in EUR, which is the local currency where the bond is issued, is considered a foreign bond in the French bond market. (Choice A) Eurobonds are debt securities issued outside of the issuer's domestic market; they are issued in one country and denominated in the currency of another. Eurobonds have numerous exemptions from local rules, regulations, and taxes that often result in lower capital costs relative to domestic bond issues. Most issuers raising capital outside of their own domestic markets do so in the Eurobond markets. (Choice C) Domestic bonds are debt securities issued within the country in which the issuer is domiciled and denominated in that country's currency. These issues are subject to local laws, regulations, and taxes. Most issued debt securities are domestic bonds.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\7. Fixed Income\7.03 Fixed-Income Issuance and Trading - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following abilities is most likely an advantage for an institutional investor participating in a bond private placement?
option_a: Influencing the terms of the transaction
option_b: Immediately reselling the bonds for a quick profit
option_c: Conducting extensive due diligence to confidently take a large portfolio position
explanation_en: Corporate bond private placements Advantages Disadvantages Influence the structure of the transaction Restricted/unregistered securities Influence covenants, collateral, etc. Riskier than most alternatives Investor Higher return potential Very limited secondary market liquidity Research intensive Small offering size limits attractiveness Reduced regulation and disclosure Small offering size Issuer Low issuance cost Higher yields Can quickly come to market Companies use many methods to issue securities when raising capital. In a private placement, bonds are sold directly to a limited number of qualified investors through a privately negotiated transaction. Common investors in private placements include pension funds and insurance companies. Private placements have several features that make them attractive to issuers, including reduced regulatory and disclosure requirements (eg, the offering is often unregistered). These features result in lower issuance costs and an ability to come to the market more quickly. Investors are attracted to the higher return potential of private placements and the ability to exert considerable influence on bond structure, collateral (ie, pledged assets), and covenants. Investors must balance these factors against the higher risks, research demands, limited liquidity, and relatively small portfolio impact of these deals. (Choice B) Since private placements are usually illiquid and come with resale restrictions, an investor is generally not able to sell immediately after purchase for a quick profit. (Choice C) Even with extensive due diligence, the relatively small size of private placements limits an institutional investor's ability to take a large position.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\7. Fixed Income\7.03 Fixed-Income Issuance and Trading - Answers.pdf
question_en: For floating-rate debt, the reference rate most likely:
option_a: defines the periodic reset of the spread.
option_b: depends mainly on the issuer's creditworthiness.
option_c: determines borrowing cost variation after issuance.
explanation_en: A floating-rate bond pays a coupon that is equal to a variable reference rate (eg, LIBOR) plus a constant spread over the reference rate. The spread is based on the issuer's creditworthiness, is set when the bond is created, and remains the same throughout the life of the bond. The higher the spread, the lower the issuer's creditworthiness. In contrast, the choice of reference rate reflects the relevant market interest rate but does not depend on the creditworthiness of the issuer (Choice B). The reference rate resets each period, which causes the coupon rate of the bond to "float" with the market rate. As a result, the reference rate determines the variation in the borrowing cost for the issuer after the bond has been issued, by defining the periodic reset of the floating rate (not the spread) (Choice A).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\7. Fixed Income\7.03 Fixed-Income Issuance and Trading - Answers.pdf
question_en: Compared with broad equity indexes (eg, STOXX Europe 600, S&P 500), broad fixed-income indexes covering the same geographic region most likely:
option_c: are equally weighted rather than market-value-weighted.
explanation_en: Fixed-income indexes vs. equity indexes Fixed income Equity National governments Regional/local governments Types of issuers Corporations Government agencies Corporations Number of issues Multiple issues per issuer Usually only 1 class of common equity Issues mature Constituent turnover Securities last for life of issuer New issues are more frequent Weighting Usually market value Usually market capitalization Broad fixed-income indexes perform the same functions for debt markets as broad equity indexes perform for stock markets. Both provide a means of tracking risk and return in different securities markets. Fixed-income indexes facilitate the evaluation of relative performance for different markets and the sectors within those markets. Indexes also serve as benchmarks for assessing the performance of investment managers and implementing indexed investment strategies. Broad fixed-income indexes differ from broad equity indexes in several significant ways. Fixed-income indexes usually contain many more securities (ie, constituents) since there are more types of issuers for debt securities (eg, governments, agencies, corporations) compared with equities, which are issued only by corporations. Furthermore, most debt issuers have multiple issues outstanding, while most corporations have only one class of common equity outstanding (Choice A). There is also much greater turnover of constituent securities in fixed-income indexes. This is due to: the more frequent issuance of new securities, which are added to the index, and the finite life of most bonds, which results in issues being removed from the index. Fixed-income indexes are usually market-value weighted, so the turnover of constituents results in these indexes reflecting changes in the composition over time (Choice C).

question_en: A negotiable certificate of deposit (CD) is best described as having:
option_a: small denominations and a penalty for early withdrawal.
option_b: a maximum maturity of one year, and interest is paid monthly.
option_c: large denominations, and it can be traded in the secondary market.
explanation_en: Certificates of deposit (CD) Nonnegotiable CD Negotiable CD Denomination ≤ USD 100,000 Usually ≥ USD 1,000,000 Early withdrawal Yes, with penalty No Tradable No Yes, in secondary market Banks receive much of their funding through retail customer deposits, but they also often turn to the wholesale funding market to obtain capital. The wholesale funding market consists of central bank funds, the interbank market, and certificates of deposit (CDs). In exchange for a deposit, a bank will issue a CD in a specific amount for a specified time and interest rate. CDs are one of the primary sources of funding for banks and similar financial institutions. CDs can be categorized as either negotiable or nonnegotiable. A nonnegotiable CD is commonly sold to the bank's retail customers. Nonnegotiable CDs pay interest at maturity, are issued in small denominations of usually less than USD 100,000, and can only be withdrawn before maturity by paying a penalty (Choice A). A negotiable CD is issued in large denominations, often USD 1 million or more, and can be traded to other investors in the secondary market. Negotiable CDs pay interest at maturity and cannot be withdrawn early. (Choice B) Both types of CDs can have maturities greater than one year. A CD with a maturity of more than one year is known as a term CD. All CDs pay interest at maturity.

question_en: A US bank issues USD 100 million in 90-day, 4% US commercial paper. Assuming a 360-day year, the proceeds from the offering (USD millions) are closest to:
explanation_en: Commercial paper is short-term unsecured debt issued by companies in many markets around the world. Commercial paper is used extensively for short-term financing needs, including working capital, seasonal funds, and bridge financing since it is relatively flexible, available, and low-cost. The United States commercial paper (USCP) market is the world's largest. Eurocommercial paper (ECP) refers to all commercial paper issued outside the United States market. One of the most important differences between these markets is the way interest is earned. USCP pays interest on a discount basis whereas the ECP market uses either an interest-bearing or discount basis. In this USCP scenario, the paper is issued at a discount to par. The interest amount is calculated as follows: For commercial paper offered on a discount basis, the offering proceeds are equal to the par value minus the interest: 100 million − 1 million = 99 million. (Choice A) USD 96 million is the result of failing to multiply by (90 ÷ 360) when calculating the interest. (Choice C) USD 100 million is the amount of proceeds if the interest of the offering were on an interest bearing (ie, yield) basis.

question_en: Interbank offered rates are least likely used:
option_a: to price a 5-year fixed-coupon bond issued by a bank.
option_b: for resetting the coupon rate on a 5-year floating-rate note (FRN)
option_c: as the reference rate for a 5-year fixed-for-floating interest rate swap.
explanation_en: Adjustable- or floating-rate instruments have numerous attractions for borrowers and creditors. Floating-rate loans or bonds are usually lower-cost sources of funds than long-term fixed rate borrowing. Lenders and investors can reduce interest rate risk by using floating-rate securities or derivatives. Interbank offered rates (eg, Libor) are widely used as reference rates for setting interest rates on such financial instruments. However, interbank rates are not used to price fixed-coupon bonds. Such a bond's price is based on the YTM at which the security is trading. A 5-year bond's price reflects a 5-year interest rate. Interbank rates have terms that range from overnight to a maximum of 1 year; therefore, they are not used to price 5-year fixed-coupon bonds. (Choices B and C) The specific interbank rate used typically has a term consistent with the reset frequency (eg, a 3-month rate is used for quarterly resets).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\7. Fixed Income\7.04 Fixed-Income Markets for Corporate Issuers - Answers.pdf
question_en: The purpose of a repo margin is most likely to:
option_a: provide a return to the lender.
option_b: shield the borrower from counterparty risk.
option_c: protect the lender from a decline in collateral value.
explanation_en: Factors affecting repo margin Collateral quality The higher the quality of collateral, the lower the margin Collateral demand Lower margin is required if specific collateral is in high demand Length The longer the term of the repo, the higher the margin Counterparty risk Higher creditworthiness of counterparty, lower margin required In a repurchase agreement ("repo"), the repo buyer, as the lender, provides cash in exchange for securities provided by the repo seller, as the borrower. In effect, securities are collateral for the short-term financing provided by the repo. The lender is exposed to the risk that the borrower will not repurchase the collateral when the agreement ends, defaulting on the repo. Although the lender can sell the collateral in the market, it is possible that its market value will have declined since the repo was initiated. To shield the lender from a decline in collateral value in the event of default, the value of the collateral is greater than the amount actually loaned (eg, 102%, 105%). The difference between the value of the collateral and the amount loaned is the repo margin. The magnitude of the repo margin depends upon: the quality of the collateral, the demand for specific collateral, the term of the repo, and the counterparty's creditworthiness. (Choice A) The lender's return (ie, interest rate) for providing cash to the borrower is the repo rate. (Choice B) The repo margin protects the lender from counterparty risk, not the borrower.

question_en: With respect to principal repayment structures, a serial maturity bond is most similar to a:
explanation_en: An issuance of corporate bonds typically has one of two principal repayment structures: In a term maturity, the entire principal amount for a bond is due on the same date. With a serial maturity, the bond issue has multiple maturity dates; the principals of certain bonds are retired on each of the maturity dates. Since a term maturity involves the issuer retiring the entire bond issue at one maturity date, it exposes bondholders to greater risk of default than a serial maturity structure. A sinking fund can mitigate this risk: the issuer is required to retire a certain minimum percentage of the bonds each year, according to a schedule designated in the bond indenture. This means that redemptions to bondholders happen over time, similarly to how cash flows occur for a bond issuance with a serial maturity structure. (Choice A) A coupon strip refers to the securities created when the interest payments from a government bond are separated ("stripped") from their principal payment and the two types of obligations trade as separate securities in the market. In this process, the date of the principal payment is not changed and occurs on the same single date, so the resulting securities are not similar to a serial maturity. (Choice B) Payment-in-kind (PIK) refers to a type of bond coupon, not a type of principal repayment structure. A PIK coupon bond pays the periodic coupon in the form of common stock shares of the company or in bonds, not cash.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\7. Fixed Income\7.04 Fixed-Income Markets for Corporate Issuers - Answers.pdf
question_en: A bank expects to originate more loans than can be funded by retail deposits. Banks in this situation most commonly utilize funding from:
explanation_en: Short-term funding available to banks Demand deposits (checking accounts) Retail deposits Savings accounts Money market accounts Central bank funds Wholesale funds Interbank deposits Certificates of deposit Short-term loan-like agreements Repurchase agreements ("repos") Repo and reverse repo Not particular to banks Debt maturities < 360 days Commercial paper Not particular to banks Financial institutions like banks have greater funding needs than nonfinancial companies since, in addition to projects like expansions and acquisitions, they engage in financial operations such as making loans and investing. Banks obtain much of their funding through the retail deposits of their customers. However, when the amount of loans made to customers exceeds the funds available from retail accounts, they most commonly turn to wholesale funds: central bank funds, interbank deposits, and certificates of deposit. Banks will use wholesale funds first, after retail deposits, since interest costs can be less than with retail deposits, repurchase agreements, and commercial paper. Wholesale funds are also important in managing any potential fixed/floating balance sheet mismatch between assets and liabilities. Repurchase agreements are another commonly used source of funds available to banks and other companies. (Choice B) Demand deposits (checking accounts) are a type of retail deposit. (Choice C) Bank financial assets tend to be relatively short-term, and therefore result in a variable rate of interest. Banks normally first turn to lower-cost wholesale funds before issuing debt in the form of bonds. If banks issue bonds, the bonds are likely to have a floating (not fixed) coupon rate.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\7. Fixed Income\7.04 Fixed-Income Markets for Corporate Issuers - Answers.pdf
question_en: For a bond issue with a sinking fund arrangement, the bonds retired prior to maturity are least likely to be retired at:
explanation_en: Sinking fund provision Predetermined schedule for retiring a portion of a bond issue prior to maturity Exposes bondholders to: Reinvestment risk Gradually reduced credit risk A bond issue with a sinking fund arrangement requires the issuer to retire a portion of the original principal amount prior to maturity (similar to a serial maturity structure). The sinking fund schedule specifies the principal amount of bonds that must be retired each year. The retirements reduce the total amount of debt outstanding, thereby reducing the credit risk faced by holders of the bonds still outstanding. The issuer can meet the sinking fund requirement by either: purchasing the required par amount in the secondary market, or randomly choosing bonds to call at par (Choice B). Bonds purchased in the secondary market must be delivered to the indenture trustee to prove compliance with the sinking fund arrangement. Secondary market purchases are used to satisfy a sinking fund retirement only if the bond is trading at a discount to par (Choice A). If the bond is trading at a premium, the sinking fund calls at par are used. Therefore, bonds with a sinking fund arrangement are unlikely to ever be retired at a premium to par.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\7. Fixed Income\7.04 Fixed-Income Markets for Corporate Issuers - Answers.pdf
question_en: A contingency provision contained in the indenture of a bond issued by a corporation most likely refers to:
option_a: the issuer's ability to defer coupon payments if certain conditions are met.
option_b: the bondholder's ability to force the corporation to redeem the bond before maturity.
option_c: the issuer's right to incur additional debt while some or all of the original amount is still
explanation_en: Typical bond contingency provisions Callability Issuer has right to redeem bond before maturity Putability Bondholder can require issuer to redeem bond before maturity Bondholder can convert bond into a predetermined number of issuer's Convertibility common shares Contingency provisions in the context of bonds are very specific and refer to the rights of the issuer and/or bondholders with respect to how a bond can be redeemed or disposed of. The most common types of contingency provisions concern whether a bond can be called, put, or converted. A putable bond gives its holder the right to require that the issuer redeem the bond before maturity. The redemption price is established in the indenture, in addition to any other relevant provisions such as when the bondholder must act. This right (ie, the put) can be valuable to the bondholder, and that value allows the issuer to pay a lower coupon rate. (Choice A) The issuer's right to defer coupon payments does not relate to redeeming or converting the bond, so it is not properly categorized as a contingency. (Choice C) Provisions concerning an issuer's ability to incur additional debt are a covenant, or promise, of actions that the issuer agrees to take (ie, affirmative covenants) or not take (ie, negative covenants).
